The $I$-band weak lensing survey from DESIY1 has yielded comprehensive catalogues of co-added images and object catalogues covering the Southern Galaxy Plane's full angular width. Building on these results, this study presents a comprehensive catalogue of large galaxies, spanning 180 degrees, that are suitable for precise galaxy orientation analysis. Utilizing a smart selection method, 1,066 galaxies are incorporated into this catalogue, each featuring an average effective radius, an additive shear bias of $3.9 \times 10^{-4}$ and a residual multiplicative shear bias of $1.1 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, this study reports an additive shear bias of $6.5 \times 10^{-4}$ for large galaxies, a residual multiplicative shear bias of $1.6 \times 10^{-4}$, and a significant correlation between ellipticity and galaxy effective radius, which may impact weak lensing analyses.

A well-known result by Erdos, Renyi and Levy reveals that, when randomly selecting an irrational number from the interval (0,1), the powers of its iterations form complete sets of integers. We consider an extension of this problem by randomly selecting n irrational numbers and forming the union of their iteration power sets, asking under what conditions the parity of certain set sizes is also randomly uniformly distributed. For n=1, this was resolved by Ruzsa and even-odd analogs were studied. Here, we show that, for any n greater than or equal to two, complete sets of integers within these set unions occur with positive probability.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain examples of k-rational and k-Du Bois classification singularities have been identified and studied.

A theoretical model is developed, in which two weakly connected Heisenberg layers interact with an external magnetic field and coupled together with a spin density wave order parameter exhibiting in-plane symmetry. A Ginzburg-Landau model is formulated, and within this framework, conditions are established for the level of interlayer coupling, magnetic interaction, and external magnetic field that favor Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations within the layers, given that this type of order parameter includes level of within-plane symmetry breaking.A numerical investigation within this model shows that within the within-plane symmetry broken state, BKT transitions occur at higher temperatures than within the case where within-plane symmetry is not broken. Additionally, when a magnetic field is applied, the model predicts lower BKT transition temperatures than would be observed in the absence of an external magnetic field.

A new version of the three-right-handed-neutrino Standard Model with one extra U(1) symmetry, termed the $a\nu$MSM, is introduced to address neutrino oscillations, combine three major particle physics problems, and provide a dark matter candidate. In this model, three major particle issues, specifically strong CP, hierarchy, and muon $g-2$ anomalies, are linked to three similar new physics sources: a pseudoscalar particle, a complex scalar, and a vector boson. Dark matter is created through a combination of three similar and vector portal mechanisms. Even though dark matter is created through three similar portal processes, dark matter is primarily controlled by the dominant of these three, which is the vector portal in most parameter spaces. The region of parameter space that can simultaneously explain the muon $g-2$ anomaly and provide the correct dark matter relic density is found to be limited. This limitation can be further restricted by future particle and cosmological observations.

The concept of stabilizer rank, a crucial measure for understanding the complexity of Wigner functions, has been refined with a novel upper bound on its rank when dealing with multiple copies of the state $|T\rangle$. This achievement surpasses previous limits on stabilizer rank, specifically showing a stabilizer rank of at most $\lceil m/3 \rceil$ and improving upon prior work that showed a rank of at most $\lfloor (m+1)/2 \rfloor$. This advancement has led to the development of an optimized decomposition of $m$ copies of $|T\rangle$ for specific cases where $m$ is a multiple of three. Furthermore, this improvement has implications for non-stabilizer state discrimination, specifically showing a notable advancement in distinguishing between different state configurations. This advancement signifies a transition from a previous distinguishing ability of $\log \log m$ to a state-of-the-art of $\log_2 m$. This enhancement has also led to a demonstration of superior performance in detecting instability of non-stabilizer states by employing a stabilizer rank-dependent detection probability.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, applying a scale factor as the infrared cutoff. Calculations are carried out for various states, including phantom ($\omega_{DE} < -1$), quintessence ($-1 < \omega_{DE} < -1/3$), and the intermediate phase ($-1/3 < \omega_{DE} < 1$). We specifically examine a critical condition where $\omega_{DE} = 1$ and investigate how this intermediate state evolves. We also analyzed the statefinder diagnostic, for both a and y, and found that both can take any real value. We determined any singularity for both the statefinder and their respective ratios, and found that both can take any real value. We found that for any real universe description, $d$ cannot be less than zero and $D$ cannot exceed a certain value. We found that both the statefinder and their respective behavior can vary depending on $d$ and $D$, and that both can take any real value.

Between January 2018 and December 2018, the LAMOST performed a unique, comprehensive two-point observation on 10,000 unique targets.  These targets were strategically arranged in a sequence that included various low- and high-resolution spectra with different signal-to-noise ratios.  The low-resolution spectra set comprised 10,000 signals, of which 81% had a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10.  The high-resolution spectra consisted of 10,000 signals, and 65% of these had a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10.  The targets were selected to include a diverse mix of objects, and the least common objects were classified as comets, asteroids, and extragalactic signals.  The scripts for data processing are freely available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/lamost/LAMOST-Science.

Previous research has shown that SRAM can be utilized to create true random numbers. A typical SRAM-based TRNG relies on SRAM's random power-down current, but its high-quality performance TRNGs are limited to a small number of bits due to their dependence on this current. To overcome this limitation, this paper presents a new method for generating large quantities of high-quality random numbers using SRAM's random switching behavior. This technique employs a random counter that is built using a chain of three SRAM cells and their leakage currents to set the initial conditions for a chain of toggle flip-flops. A novel approach is taken to filter out the meta-stability of these cells by using the sum of their leakage currents to set the initial conditions for a random counter. By utilizing a ring oscillator as a time base, the counter is incremented until a predetermined condition is met. When this happens, a snapshot is taken of the counter's value, which is then used as the output random number. This process is then repeated with different random settings provided by the counter's sum of leakage currents, which enables generation of large quantities of random numbers. To verify the randomness of the generated numbers, two advanced statistical tests are used to assess the quality of the output data.

A pioneering electronic device, the memristor, has the capability to store information as a persistent electrical current, which is dependent on previously supplied currents. We have developed a reliable method for fabricating Resistor Random Access Memory (RRAM) by utilizing molecular structures that undergo a process called electrochemical reaction. Using a novel molecular compound, 1-(2-(2-phenylvinyl)phenyl)ammonium chloride vapor, we have achieved the ability to create entirely functional, single-molecule memory devices that operate at temperatures below 50 Celsius, with a structure size smaller than 10 nanometers. This new material exhibits the necessary properties for memory application, including the ability to store information, switch states, and retain data without power. Our findings have been further enhanced by developing multi-bit encoding, allowing the memory device to store multiple bits. This work represents the first instance of memory application using 2D materials.

The concept of loop-tree duality (LTD) has emerged as a promising method for streamlining the calculation of complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes. A series of studies have demonstrated its potential by applying it to specific cases, namely the L-loop L-point vacuum vacuum graph and certain two-loop examples. This work extends those findings by applying LTD to the computation of two-loop planar and non-planar heavy quark mass corrections within scalar theory.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for a class of quantum walks. We focus on a general model of two-state quantum walks with periodic movements. Our work builds upon and generalizes previous findings for specific types of equations, such as the discrete Schrödinger equation, by considering more complex scenarios where the momentum is not uniform. We also explore the relationship between our work and other relevant studies in the field.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

This study investigates $q$-deformed three-mode optomechanical systems to explore phase transitions through a mathematical model of light interacting with two mirrors. The conventional system exhibits a smooth transition from continuous phase transitions, whereas its $q$-deformed counterpart displays a sudden change at a critical point. Introducing a control parameter in the model allows us to analyze how $q$-deformation impacts optomechanical phase transitions. The research reveals that as $q$-deparation increases, the critical values for several order parameters shift to lower values. Additionally, we utilize the order parameter to analyze how varying $q$-deformation influences its symmetry. Our findings demonstrate that not only can deformation induce phase transitions, but the extent of this deformation also significantly influences its characteristics.

In a previous study, I demonstrated that the Two-Rotors Model can produce R-negative scissors states using classically interlocked structures, which have one element larger than the other. Building upon this work, I examined a scenario in which the smaller element matches the size of the larger one, resulting in two equally sized components. Under these conditions, I discovered that it is impossible to achieve R-negative scissors states, as no configuration can be found that satisfies the required properties for these states to occur.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly altered due to their two-dimensional structure. A method is presented that uses a magnetized sputtering technique to create a multi-functional 2D interface between a ferromagnetic material and a ferroelectric material. This technique utilizes a magnetized target to ferrotoroidization and a magnetized coil to adjust the ferroelectric properties at a specific location within a manganite/lead-zirconate-titanate system. A observed increase of 30 K is found in the electric-field-induced resistive switching temperature when using an optimally balanced magnetization configuration, which is attributed to the increased stability of the ferromagnetic phase in the thin film.

The occurrence of diffusion can be recognized across various systems, both natural and man-made. In this paper, an example of anomalous diffusion is presented, which is often associated with complex systems exhibiting memory effects. This case of anomalous diffusion is analyzed by a company's decision-making process, which is modeled as a system with memory. It is demonstrated that this man-made system exhibits the characteristics of an anomalous diffusion.

This study explores whether stable coins serve as a refuge from volatility in cryptocurrency markets. Initially, we investigate stable coins through the lens of high-order statistical interconnections within a cryptocurrency network. The results reveal that stable coins play a crucial role, acting as stability anchors for other cryptocurrencies. Subsequently, we examine which cryptocurrency investors rely upon to mitigate the effects of cryptocurrency instability. The analysis indicates that within major cryptocurrency subsets, specific cryptocurrencies function as stable points of reference for other assets.

The widespread adoption of open-source software necessitates consistent, automated, and real-time testing to ensure the continued functionality of existing tests and integration with new modules. To this end, we introduce a script called a tester, written in Python, which streamlines the testing process by compiling a list of tests to run, executing them, and summarizing the results. This simple yet effective tool is already in use at the Max-Planck Institute for Meteorology, where it has been successfully applied to validate cloud modeling software, including the WRF-Chem model.

We establish a novel definition of a compact perception pair, demonstrating its equivalence to total boundedness of a specific measurement space. Furthermore, we develop a corresponding compact perception hierarchy, alongside a novel algorithm and theoretical analysis to facilitate the construction of this pair. The framework of our algorithm is then applied to solve extension issues associated with optimal perception hierarchy construction and traffic flow estimation problems.

The behavior of transverse energy currents in crystalline solids is influenced by the electronic band structure's geometry.  However, this phenomenon is not only a property of uniform systems, but also a feature that persists when a gravitational potential is applied.  Research has been conducted to investigate how transverse energy currents occur in two types of materials, specifically bismuth and tungsten, within the context of the Dirac and Kawakubo models.  When mock gauge fields are introduced into these materials, resulting energy currents are observed that adhere to specific theoretical predictions.  Notably, these energy currents are independent of mass terms present in these models.  Additionally, certain deviations from these energy currents are found to align with quanta-based calculations.

In various machine learning domains, there's a growing emphasis on model simplicity, where complexity is often measured by generalization performance, which is influenced by a model's capacity. Within deep learning, capacity is commonly assessed using the number of parameters. We propose that a more pertinent form of simplicity may be found in a model's manifold structure, a concept we term geometric complexity. Our investigation focuses on whether a reduced model, with fewer parameters, can achieve equivalent performance to a larger one, through alterations in its geometric complexity. Specifically, by employing two methods, we modify the geometric complexity of ResNet models and observe that these changes indeed facilitate better performance in a smaller-sized model, outperforming its larger counterparts despite having fewer parameters. Our studies also reveal that a model's geometric complexity has a significant impact on its performance beyond the manifold of images.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations. Our analysis focuses on the CMS dataset from $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV, corresponding to 1 ${\rm fb}^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. Results indicate the potential for precise Wilson coefficient estimation through improved detection capabilities and analysis techniques.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite numerous attempts, models have struggled to match human scorers.  Recent breakthroughs in language processing, particularly with transformer-based models, have provided a pathway to improved solutions.  This study evaluates the effectiveness of combining specific language models and the impact of data preprocessing on self-supervised models for the task of automated essay grading.  Through our experiments, we discovered that utilizing a single, carefully processed dataset with the right transformer model can lead to significant performance gains.  In our testing, our best model achieved an correlation score of 0.4604, and we attribute a substantial 0.1177 improvement to data preprocessing.  Additionally, we released the corresponding code on GitHub for reference.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system is a crucial driver of social progression.  It's essential to examine whether this dynamic has improved over the past few decades, especially in light of the significant expansions in higher education opportunities that have taken place within Brazil, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Japan, and Sweden.  A significant barrier to assessing intergenerational mobility via higher education arises from a lack of data on parents' educational backgrounds.  However, the utilization of information from three distinct sources - data on individuals' life experiences, registries of university students, and census records - enables researchers to explore this issue.  Our analysis reveals that, although there have been substantial increases in higher education opportunities over the past few decades, intergenerational mobility within these countries has remained consistent.  Notably, our findings suggest that the recent expansions in higher education opportunities have not necessarily led to a decline in intergenerational mobility.  Instead, our research suggests the existence of an underlying mechanism that can simultaneously account for both the observed increases in opportunities and the stability of mobility patterns.  This mechanism appears to involve an equilibrium in which the number of individuals entering higher education and the number of available jobs are in balance.  As a result, the proportion of individuals from different family backgrounds entering higher education and the available job market remains consistent.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in a specific way. Furthermore, a formula for calculating any particle exchange statistic within the boson/fermi system is presented in the form of an equation.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports Steal-From-Any and Spend-From-Any transactions, which are crucial for various applications such as multi-signature setups, chaff keys, and transparent and confidential refund methods. The-Project/Delegated-RingCT is a compact and code-efficient solution, with no project-specific structure, that can be seamlessly integrated into Logarithlink, Chaco-Link, Groestlcoin, Zcash, and similar cryptocurrencies based on Tacit coins.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings show that recent achievements in solving certain types of systems, such as those described by certain matrices, can be extended to other types of matrices with similar properties. This discovery has significant implications for personalizing quantum algorithms aimed at solving linear systems within the quantum RAM model. Our research builds on recent breakthroughs in quantum algorithms in order to demonstrate these implications.

Researchers have made the initial observation of three massive gauge bosons being produced simultaneously in high-energy collisions between protons.  Specifically, simultaneous occurrences of bostrons, W bosons and Z bosons are observed with a total of 5 significant standard deviations when all possible arrangements of their charges are combined, and a 6 significant standard deviation observation for positive charge arrangements specifically.  These observations of individual events exceed standard model projections by significant margins, ranging from 2 to 15 significant standard deviations, depending on the arrangement of charges.  Subsequent statistical analyses have also revealed multiple instances of other unusual phenomena to occur as well, such a significant top quark appearing in certain interactions, top quark spins aligned in a particular manner and a top quark appearing alone in others.  These various analyses have a significance ranging from 2 to 3 significant standard deviations from what is expected in standard model interactions.  To better understand these unusual phenomena, researchers have also examined potential influences of new, unusual physical phenomena that could be responsible for these observations.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus is now shown to contain numerous inaccuracies and is limited in size, which hinders learning effective language models. These issues are further complicated by the fact that most NLP models are trained using the same flawed corpus. This research paper is the first of its kind to apply modern Hebrew NLP tasks, which are typically associated with other languages. Specifically, the authors investigate the effectiveness of training on the flawed corpus versus creating and training on a new, more accurate annotated treebank. Additionally, the authors explore the development of a high-quality error-free dataset, which will serve as a benchmark for evaluating Hebrew NLP performance.

We maintain fixed $p \in [1,\infty)$ and $K \in (0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\mu$ on a product of $N$ intervals. A fundamental challenge in artificial neural networks is the catastrophic forgetting issue, which hinders current networks from acquiring new, unrelated information without erasing previously learned associations. In contrast, humans can effortlessly acquire various skills and remember previous knowledge. To address this problem, researchers have been exploring continual learning techniques. In this study, we present an innovative approach called LF-ECN that overcomes forgetting problems and facilitates continual learning. Proposed to enhance learning speed, we employ an excitatory/inhibitory architecture within our neural networks. Our method also enables the model to accurately predict previously learned tasks during the learning process of subsequent, unrelated tasks, which is a capability not present in other networks.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly generated low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of edge connections and degree distributions. This study differs by investigating LDPC codes constructed through a latent variable model, which incorporates correlations between vertex degrees. Notably, our analysis reveals that correlations between vertex degrees in LDPC codes significantly impact their performance, particularly their erasure thresholds when decoded using a binary message-passing algorithm over a binary erasure channel. Furthermore, our findings indicate that certain correlations can increase the erasure threshold, while others decrease it. These results distinguish randomly generated LDPC codes from previously studied models, such as the bipartite Erdos-Renyi graph model, and provide a framework for generating high-performance LDPC codes.

A novel method, the safety-scheduled improved model predictive safety filter, is proposed to enhance existing model predictive safety filter designs. This approach aims to expand the range of situations in which the filter can operate effectively while maintaining the same level of control performance. Furthermore, a more efficient computational procedure is developed, reducing processing demands and enabling application to a broader array of practical systems. Under specific conditions, it is proven that the developed filter guarantees system safety.

A critical vulnerability exists in current quantum key distribution implementations, stemming from non-ideal device behavior. This vulnerability could enable attackers to circumvent security protocols. This research proposes an innovative approach to protect against such device imperfections by harnessing error correction and predictive techniques. The method involves having a legitimate communicating party anticipate faults and have a supporting party predict errors introduced by an adversary. The outcomes of these interactions are incorporated into error correction and secret distillation processes. Although adversaries could exploit these interactions to gather information, their overall access remains limited. The effectiveness of this strategy is demonstrated through numerical simulations, which highlight its potential benefits. Additionally, the error prediction channel can be utilized as a useful resource. The proposed framework may also be applied to other applications, such as blinding attacks in quantum key distribution.

Recent studies have highlighted in-context learning (ICL) as a capability of large-scale language models, allowing them to adapt to various tasks through a few examples provided in the form of prompts. Despite the widespread use of general-purpose corpora like Wikipedia and common news articles as pretraining data, the impact of specific training sources on ICL performance has received little attention. In this study, we investigate how different training corpora influence ICL by analyzing the performance of our developed corpus-controlled pretraining models. We find that models trained on diverse, internet-based data outperform those using conventional corpora in previous research. Moreover, our study reveals that internet-trained models not only excel in ICL with examples from their own training data but also demonstrate superior performance with examples outside of their training distribution.

Galaxy cluster observations have provided evidence for large, persistent cold clouds within the hot intra-cluster medium. Although models based on cooling and feedback processes can reproduce a significant portion of this data, they struggle to explain the growth and evolution of these clouds. We propose an alternative model in which the inner regions of galaxy clusters host a central supermassive black hole that is surrounded by a dynamically important, torus-shaped cold cloud. As the central black hole accretes mass, it expels the cloud using powerful jets, causing it to fragment and create further cooling. We present 3D hydrodynamic simulations showing the growth and jet-driven disruption of these clouds, as well as their interaction with the hot ICM. We find that the simulated gas distribution matches observational data, and our model is consistent with data on cluster cores, radio lobes and jets, and the mass distribution of off-nuclei galaxies.

The investigation into CPT symmetry, which is closely linked to fundamental principles in particle physics, provides an excellent opportunity for thoroughly examining the predictions of the Standard Model. The study of CPT-violating phenomena in b hadrons, particularly their decay processes, allows for more sensitive testing of the standard model than other areas, making it a crucial area of research. This paper summarizes recent findings on CPT-violating phenomena within the context of particle physics and reports on the progress made at the LHCb experiment, focusing primarily on the study of CP-violating phenomena, as CPT and CP violations are often difficult to distinguish apart.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of these newly discovered amplitudes matches the sum of two previously established types.

The emerging mobile networks will heavily rely on diverse applications such as augmented reality, virtual reality, and the internet of vehicles, which will place immense pressure on future networks' resources. To effectively support these new services, advanced forecasting and optimization techniques will be crucial for efficient resource management. Our research focuses on developing and applying machine learning-based methods for real-time resource provisioning. Specifically, we utilize reinforcement learning to tackle complex multi-objective problems through the development of a unified framework. This framework is exemplified by our work in virtualizing network functions and optimizing cloud radio access network resource allocation.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a voice from minimal training data, specifically as few as one second of audio. Existing methods, such as Acoustic Unit Selection (AUS) and Speech Waveform Generation, have achieved success with synthesis durations of 10-20 seconds. However, the current duration limit hinders their applicability in practical scenarios. To address this, we present ZeroSpeech++, an enhanced zero-speech synthesis system aiming to push the boundary of synthesizing a voice with as little as one second of training audio over a minute or more of text. To reach this goal, we introduce: 1) ZeroSpeech++ speech recognition training with 100k additional hours of data, 2) A novel acoustic unit system based on 10ms frames called Psuedo Phrases (Ps), which significantly reduces the number of required training audio segments. With this innovation, we can increase the variety of acoustic units while maintaining the number of required samples. 3) A novel AUS model called Enc-Dec AUS that can effectively use Ps to synthesize a voice. 4) A new Speech Waveform Generation approach called Wave-GAN-VITS+ which outperforms previous versions in terms of quality. With these advancements, we demonstrate the ability to synthesize a minute-long speech over a minute-long training audio with high accuracy.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints is a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often plagued by local solutions and convergence failures. We present a novel optimization approach that guarantees a force-feasible solution within a specific range, using an efficient method with multiple starting points. This methodology incorporates boundary reduction, a branch-and-bound framework, and a quick elimination technique to exclude impossible intervals. Numerical simulations demonstrate the algorithm's capabilities.

We examine how to transform one quantum state into another using a quantum resource theory, focusing on a non-quantizing quantum channel model. In this theory, we establish that a key condition for physically transforming one state into another is also both necessary and sufficient for its optimality. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form calculation for the optimal conversion probability. This mathematical relationship also enables us to efficiently solve the optimal state conversion and purification conversion problems, which we demonstrate on a specific theory model, allowing for a direct solution to the optimal quantum state purification problem.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in a nonlinear system, similar to a driven pendulum.  This is achieved by establishing two key methods for analyzing the stability and limit cycles that arise as a result of parameter variations.  These methods involve utilizing a technique to simplify complex equations and another technique based on perturbation analysis to approximate solutions.  Our findings demonstrate that these analytical methods can accurately predict the system's behavior, specifically how parametric excitation can cause instability and lead to a variety of limit cycle patterns.  To further examine the system's behavior, we utilize numerical simulations and a three-dimensional plot to visualize the various limit cycle patterns.  Our research provides a framework for analyzing the complex behavior of coupled systems and has potential applications in fields such as fluid dynamics.

In our research, we introduce a new communication-efficient technique for training
machine learning models across a network of interconnected devices. By integrating
two concepts, specifically bias-reduced communication and a robust statistical
model, our method, known as Distributionally Robust Decentralized Stochastic Gradient
Descent (DR-DSGD), enhances the efficiency of communication within distributed
learning. By minimizing a theoretically determined communication cost at each step,
our approach hedges against potential data distribution disparities among devices.
Comparative experiments with Vondrick-DSGD and Avg-DSGD demonstrate the efficacy
of our communication-saving method, with improvements of up to 10 times in Driven
Autonomous System training and a similar level of acceleration in Decentralized
System training.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a connection between initial energy states and最终的 particle counts in high-energy collisions. The research focuses on 1+1 dimensional systems with massless particles, examining how energy deposition influences the production of particles as system parameters move away from relativistic symmetry. By combining an advanced mathematical model with experimental data, the study reveals that a significant portion of particles are produced during the early stages of the collision, and this relationship varies with system parameters. Additionally, the research indicates that non-relativistic behaviors exhibit a distinct threshold, below which particle counts decrease exponentially. The findings are applied to data from high-energy collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, yielding a minimum estimate for initial system temperatures.

Using sophisticated computer simulations, researchers have investigated how protostellar jets behave under the influence of a strong magnetic field and compare their properties to observations of young star forming regions. The study reveals that the magnetic field strength significantly impacts jet formation and dynamics. Specifically, the magnetic field suppresses accretion, causes the magnetosphere to shrink and move closer to the central star, and the accretion disk is compressed and moved to larger distances. The predicted jets from the simulation align with observed jets in terms of collimation, velocity, and interaction with surrounding dusty envelopes. The simulation also reveals a kiloparsec-scale jet structure with embedded knots, corresponding to the observed pattern in TW Hydrae. The findings imply that protostellar age observations from radioactive isotopes may be biased towards younger ages due to increased jet activity and increased envelope dust at later stages of development. The comparison with previous simulation findings suggests a transition in radio emission behavior, from being dominated by shock interaction in early stages to being enhanced by synchrotron emission in later stages of development.

This study investigates the balance between performance and system saturation in a series of nonlinear systems that have constraints, utilizing a performance-safety assessment approach. It's often necessary to reduce input to prevent saturation, yet this can lead to suboptimal performance. To address this, we evaluate different levels of safety reduction, which have varying impacts on performance, to identify a secure yet efficient input. Our research begins by defining a performance-safety assessment metric for each performance vector, based on the maximum allowable input without saturation. This metric is then utilized to assess the various trade-offs between performance and security. Ultimately, we use these assessments to develop a series of constraints that can be applied to each input to ensure safety. These constraints, although individually conservative, collectively provide an effective means of preventing saturation without significantly affecting performance. Our research is conducted within a model-predictive framework in which a performance-optimization step is followed by a security assessment step. Our approach is demonstrated using two nonlinear systems, a balance control for a ball on a beam and a speed control for a vehicle.

This research investigates the equilibrium points of objects with a high area-to-mass ratio, considering the Earth's shape and solar radiation pressure. It demonstrates that the oblateness of the Earth has a significant impact, causing the equilibrium points to shift and change position, particularly for objects with specific physical properties. Furthermore, the study develops an algorithm to identify stable equilibrium points and certain regions that maintain stability over time. It also identifies conditions that ensure long-term stability and provides a method for calculating these conditions. Numerical examples are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the research.

We examine the performance of velocity and dipole tight-binding models in describing many-body wavepacket dynamics within a light-matter system. Our findings indicate the velocity model can accurately simulate wavepacket evolution, but requires a strong electromagnetic field to do so. In contrast, the dipole model, which tends to describe wavepacket motion via a semi-classical approach, successfully replicates the stationary state behavior using an external field. We develop a novel testing procedure to evaluate the level of external field dependence in tight-binding models. Our research guides further development of TB models that can accurately simulate wavepacket dynamics under a weaker external electromagnetic influence.

In a specific challenge, our goal is to determine the 3D pose and shape of point clouds within a set, given that examples exist outside of that set. To address this issue, which arises due to the variability in the point clouds' appearance, we propose a two-step approach that utilizes self-supervised learning. Firstly, our method employs self-supervised 3D data augmentation to generate a varied dataset for training a shared encoder, enabling it to distinguish between intra-class variations and maintain the class's general shape. Next, our approach introduces a novel module for decoding pose and shape, which is then used to define a loss function that aligns the encoded manifold with the trained encoder. By applying our approach to several datasets, we demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing various aspects of 3D object shapes and provide comprehensive evaluations of its performance in understanding shape, pose, and synthetic data generation.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups with similar vulnerabilities but different causes of disease. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to borrow information across these subgroups. The new method has higher statistical power compared to a traditional frequentist approach, which is often used, and it requires less sample size to achieve the same level of power when the new treatment shows a consistent effect across the subgroups. However, if the new treatment shows varying effects across the subgroups, both higher power and a smaller sample size are needed to detect the difference. The performance of this new method is consistent when the new treatment shows varying effects across the subgroups. The approach is further illustrated through a simulated trial testing a new therapeutic protein in four subgroups of cancer.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now satisfy stringent accuracy requirements in a minimal space with rapid cycle times. The current method of control design involves creating multiple controllers and tuning them separately, which in practice seldom yields the ideal results due to unavoidable coupling between axes. This research introduces a novel control technique that employs a single multi-variable controller to suppress the interaction between axes in motion systems with multiple degrees of freedom. The control method is then applied to advanced motion systems and compared with the traditional approach of tuning each axis independently.

We introduce a novel, fully differentiable approach to aligning partially visible, incomplete point clouds. Our method leverages a neural network-based detector to identify key points and their corresponding tangent directions on objects. These key points are then optimized using an alignment objective function that accounts for detection errors along with a geometric registration constraint. This constraint utilizes a local graph-based matching method that ensures robust alignment even when object parts are only partially visible. Our framework is built on two neural components: a keypoint detector capable of handling partial observations and a Local Global Alignment Network (LGA-Net) that produces matching scores based on local geometry and global alignment information. l

A group G is said to exhibit property $R_\infty$ if all possible field extensions result in an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes for any non-trivial automorphism within the group. The research presents a construction that confirms the existence of a countably limitless number of countably generated metabelian groups that do not satisfy $R_\infty$ but do satisfy $R_2$ (which denotes that all fields over the group result in infinite classes for the specific automorphism id - end). Additionally, it is proven that for solvable groups of degree two, the properties $R_\infty$ and $R_2$ are equivalent. Furthermore, it is shown that for metabelian groups, $R_\infty$ implies that the group possesses property AM (which denotes the existence of a finite field over the group for every non-trivial automorphism).

This review provides an overview of the relationship between high-energy physics and the current account, with a particular emphasis on how fundamental physical parameters such as the strong interaction, Higgs boson mass, and top quark mass influence the stability of the Higgs potential. The article also explores potential avenues to detect new physics through the production of top quarks and discusses the potential implications of deviations from the Standard Model predictions on high-energy physics and global financial stability.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental findings. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, which have not been previously computed. The method of local Lorentz covariance is employed, and it is shown to simplify the calculation by minimizing unnecessary computations.

We investigate higher-order Sobolev spaces with periodic boundary conditions, particularly focusing on whether certain Sobolev spaces are non-trivial. It is shown that a specific condition must be met for these spaces to be non-trivial. With the exception of one case, it had been known previously that the condition meets the requirement. This note addresses the exceptional exception. It also demonstrates that a different set of, more stringent, conditions would also result in non-trivial Sobolev spaces.

Segmenting new, unseen imaging modalities is a relatively simple task if the other two dimensions (image and ground truth) are available for training. However, dealing with a new labeling modality that either doesn't have a corresponding label or is difficult to obtain, poses significant challenges. Furthermore, if the new labeling modality has a different definition of what constitutes an object, standard segmentation techniques may not apply.

To address this issue, a new self-supervised method called Self-Guided Attention is proposed, which can be used for segmenting previously unlabelled or difficult-to-label imaging modalities. It only requires the existing imaging modality and doesn't involve any loss related to a labeling modality.

Experimental results on synthetic images with two distinct labeling modalities, as well as real-world histology and immunofluorescence images, demonstrate the effectiveness of Self-Guided Attention in adapting to new labeling modalities and achieving segmentations as good as those obtained using self-supervised methods with the original modality and the label.

Our proposed algorithm, based on a new RNN architecture, can accurately predict action classes from a single action instance. It also has a novel capability to anticipate discrete future action features, which we've found to be useful for generating a concise action description. The RNN takes action features as input, which are either manually extracted or obtained through a single frame of action video, and is then trained using a action class label along with additional parameters. We've developed a specific RNN model that can both memorize input action features and learn to predict action classes. The results of our experiments using this RNN model have demonstrated outstanding performance in action prediction and future feature generation. The generated action features can be used to create action descriptions, which we've found to be more precise than those produced by other methods.

Hundreds of white-light stellar flares have been identified in recent years through space telescopes such as Kepler and TESS, which have led to significant advancements in our understanding of how these flares impact exoplanets. Given that wide-scale space missions like TESS are continuously discovering new planets, particularly those orbiting within their host star's habitable zone, it is essential to consider the effects of stellar flares when evaluating these exoplanets for potential biosignatures. To contribute to this objective, this research focuses on assessing the habitability of planets located in the habitable zones of M-dwarf stars, which are the most frequently discovered star type. To accomplish this, a mathematical model is employed to simulate the radiation emitted by a typical M-dwarf star during a flare, taking into account various flare parameters such as peak intensity, spectral slope, and energy distribution. The model is then utilized to estimate the dosage of X-ray and extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation that would be received by a planet in the habitable zone of an M-dwarf star, and this dosage is compared to a safe limit that would be encountered by a planet in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, which allows us to define the deformation map for nearly parallel G2 structures using spinors. We give an example of an 8-dimensional nearly G2-manifold that has a non-trivial cohomology group, $H^1(M,\mathbb{R})$.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a specific condition under commutation with complex scalar multiplication. Specifically, $T$ is C-normal if $TT^* = \alpha T^*T$ for some positive scalar $\alpha$ that is either $1$ or $0 < \alpha < 1$. While C-normal operators were first defined by Li in 2019 and initially explored with normality in mind, recent research has primarily focused on properties of C-normal matrices. In this study, we investigate the normality, C-normality, and 2-isometry properties of sums and products of operators, under conditions where $A$ is a C-normal operator, $B$ is a normal operator, or both.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study focuses on p-core p'-partitions which don't include any parts divisible by p. Notably, the analysis is carried out in the context of fields whose characteristic is not equal to p. Lacking a combinatorial representation, these p-core p'-partitions appear as coefficients in a modified version of the hook-content formula. A key finding of the study is the demonstration of functional equations for a family of p-core p'-partitions.

Neural network-based point cloud models are typically trained using either region-based or end-to-end approaches, but both methods have a major drawback - they require models with a high number of parameters. As a result, these models struggle when encountering common 3D transformations. A solution to this problem is presented in the form of a framework called ShiftNet, which applies shift-based layers to accommodate points within a shift region. This shift-based mechanism enables ShiftNet to handle a broad range of 3D transformations, including rigid body transformations as well as non-uniform scaling. Evaluations using the KITTI and NuScenes datasets show that ShiftNet, when integrated with regional and end-to-end models, outperforms their standard versions in terms of 3D object localization performance.

We examine the Clear Channel Assessment (CCA) success rate in Cooperative Sense-Multiple Access (CSMA) radar networks, taking into account the finite bandwidth of radio frequency signals. We develop a theoretical model that relates CCA success rate to system parameters and show that this model accurately matches simulations. The Model's capability to quantify CCA success in a finite bandwidth environment enables a coherent analysis of CSMA performance, which we utilize to investigate the correlation between CCA outcomes and CSMA efficiency. Our study employs a multi-metric assessment to evaluate CSMA, including throughput, packet delay, and a comprehensive utility index that integrates the CMA success rate and a node's data transmission opportunities. The results reveal a non-monotonic correlation between these metrics, suggesting an optima point exists for packet delay and overall utility under specific conditions. Additionally, we investigate how increasing system size affects this optimum point and identify key design considerations for CSMA-based radar applications.

Our investigation involves a theoretical examination of the interaction of entangled photons, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, with a Raman active material.
A Raman active material is characterized by a lack of light absorption at the Raman shift frequency, allowing for the exploration of how this interaction affects photon correlations.
We analyze this effect by investigating how the Raman interaction influences both first- and second-order correlations of signal and idler photons, as well as how it affects signal-idler photon correlations at two distinct frequencies.
This research sheds light on the impact of Raman scattering on correlated photons, providing an in-depth understanding of this phenomenon at various levels.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre99 has a greather structure than previously thought, and by further demonstrating that T-equivariant theory of $\mathcal{E}_\infty$-ring spectra can be used to define analogous structures for stacks $\mathcal{M}_\infty^{\mathcal{E}_\infty}(G,T,S^1)_{\mathcal{M}_\infty^{\mathcal{E}_\infty}(G,T,S^1)}$ of $\mathcal{E}_\infty$-rings, as shown in BHK20. We apply this development to compute cohomology rings of complex projective spaces and Grassmannians, using these results to identify the $\mathcal{E}_\infty$-structure on $H_{\mathcal{E}_\infty}^*(CP(V))$.

Temporal knowledge graph reasoning has recently gained significant attention due to the increasing application of event and time-slated knowledge graph embeddings. 
  A prominent technique for generating these embeddings is the knowledge graph completion method. 
  This study evaluates the effectiveness of this approach on a diverse set of temporal knowledge graphs, comparing various graph representation algorithms. 
  We also devise and employ a new decoding method to enhance the efficiency of graph completion models trained with the traditional stochastic gradient descent technique. 
  This approach allows models to be trained on temporal knowledge graphs, which can be either dense or heterogeneous in structure. 
  Our findings reveal that the knowledge graph completion method is effective for temporal data, with a level of performance comparable to other approaches. 
  Moreover, we observe that the optimal graph model varies depending on the specific task at hand. 
  In contrast to research on event and time-slated knowledge graph embeddings, which primarily rely on neural networks, our analysis indicates that simpler models may be more easily understood.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked, resulting in simulations that do not meet expectations. To improve this, we develop a method to calculate the sound produced by the ground during an impact, making it audible to humans. The sound waves generated by the ground propagate through the air, and their relationship with the impact is such that they can be perceived before the object itself moves. By using a mouse as a case study, we identify the key factors that make ground sound noticeable in synthesis, including the sound pressure level, frequency content, and the fact that it can be heard prior to the object's movement. The proposed method successfully recreates ground sound in a way that is more similar to the acoustic signal of a real impact, addressing the limitations of existing synthesis techniques.

A prevalent notion exists that 'always-type' all-versus-nothing (AVN) proofs in nature solely arise from correlations that are both deterministic and quantum in nature, as confirmed by experiments. However, our findings disprove this hypothesis. We demonstrate that correlations which are stochastic yet genuinely quantum can also lead to 'always-type' all-versus-nothing proofs, as validated by a thought experiment. We then illustrate a real-stochastic correlation-based all-versus-nothing proof through a study of a Higgs bose-matheson device. Our study further includes an analysis of correlations that are partially deterministic or quantum in nature. We also explore scenarios where local randomness can be exploited and provide a new example of stochastic correlations that lead to 'always-type' all-versus-nothing proofs. Our work emphasizes the significance of considering real-stochastic correlations in foundational research.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, known as XLBH$_3$, has been found to potentially surpass MgB$_2$ as a superconductor. This unique lattice structure features a hexagonal pattern with an additional hydrogen atom, resulting in substantial in-plane stiffness. Initial research has produced a hydrogen boride superconducting material that is not a superconductor, however. Hydrogen within XLBH$_3$ can be substituted, however. When sub-stoichiometric hydrogen is present, this compound becomes a superconductor. Substituting with more than one hydrogen per formula unit results in a ferromagnetic state. Using first-principles calculations, we found that phonon interactions within XLBH$_3$ are capable of forming a superconducting gap. Substituted versions of the material, specifically fXLBH$_3$ and XLBH$_3$^+$, were also found to be potential superconductors. Notably, fXLBH$_3$ exhibits a significantly higher isoscalar density compared to Sr$_2$CuO$_2$ and Pb, suggesting that it could potentially become a high-temperature superconductor.

Research on the division of objects into non-empty groups, known as partitions, is a fundamental area of combinatorial mathematics that has significant implications in computer science, particularly in the analysis of complex networks. To expand on existing existing division methods, researchers have introduced a novel type of partition called "flattened partitions." By doing so, they established a one-to-one correspondence between these flattened partitions and a specific number identified by a reference system. Furthermore, the study examined specific categories of flattened partitions resulting from the addition of new elements to existing divisions, ultimately discovering that these partitions correspond to another set of numbers defined by a research classification system.
