u_\ell 
u_\ell h'$ and $	extrm{gh}	o h'
u_\ell 
u_\ell h''$, where the intermediate states of $h'$ and $h''$ decay into various final states. These are then combined after imposing a mass constraint to estimate the Higgs boson pair mass $M_{HH}$. The simulation considers two different constraints, a 5% and a 1% mass resolution, and calculates the effectiveness of various analysis techniques to distinguish $M_{HH}$ distributions from the standard model background.

A novel method is introduced to tackle single-view 3D object pose estimation using in-the-wild videos, which are characterized by diverse camera viewpoints, object orientations, and challenging lighting conditions.  In this approach, a fast and efficient 3D pose estimator is trained to directly predict pose parameters from image input, leveraging a well-optimized pipeline of video extraction, frame augmentation, and processing.  Initial experiments on a custom dataset of in-the-wild videos demonstrate the potential of this method to provide real-time, accurate three-dimensional object pose estimation in complex environments.

This theoretical framework analyzes how individuals respond to misinformation surrounding COVID-19 vaccines by integrating concepts from information systems and social psychology. The model explores how fear stemming from a pandemic influences the rejection of misinformation, which in turn impacts both vaccine hesitancy and support. By introducing a mechanism for the diffusion of information systems, the model provides a foundation for understanding how different individuals make decisions regarding vaccination and can be adapted to various contexts by modifying the coefficients and functions involved.

Advancements in attosecond science hold immense promise, and their development relies heavily on achieving specific technological objectives: high-order harmonic sources must be both highly efficient and capable of generating multi-terahertz fields. The interaction of these fields with electrons enables researchers to probe systems on extremely short timescales, ultimately leading to the creation of attosecond pulses. A novel approach utilizing a gas-filled corner-cube resonator has been demonstrated, which reflects a femtosecond laser beam and generates a standing wave. The interaction with the gas within the resonance region produces not only efficient XUV harmonics but also attosecond bursts driven by multi-terahertz fields. The synergy between these fields allows for the exploration of new phenomena and the realization of novel research possibilities.

Eclipse prediction models for binary stars are generally accurate, 
except in cases where the orbit is decaying. This happens when the 
system loses mass and angular momentum. As a result, some binary stars 
show periodic changes in their eclipse times. These changes can be 
caused by the presence of a third body that induces a 3-body orbit. 
This paper explores creating more precise eclipse prediction models by 
considering the effects of orbital perturbation. A new Java-based web 
application called 'Eclipse Calculator' was developed to accurately 
calculate eclipse times for periodic and perturbed systems. This tool can 
be accessed at the following link: https://www.ing.infn.it/~frecini/ephem/

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under conditions of focusing nonlinearity, exceeding the critical mass level, and solutions with negative total energy. We show that for a wide range of scenarios, such solutions become unbounded as time progresses, and can become completely unstable. A key aspect of our research involves developing a novel, more flexible version of a gradient flow, making it possible to define distinct target sets for different situations. We also define specific sets of unstable states for each scenario, and demonstrate that solutions starting in these states will become unstable.

Physics-informed neural networks offer a promising solution for tackling partial differential equations by integrating mathematical expressions with data-driven approaches. However, determining which parts of the network to optimize has been a longstanding challenge. Although some solutions exist, they fall short when applied to certain types of PDEs. In contrast, a universal optimization strategy can accommodate various cases. In addition, a comparison of different training methods reveals that a specific technique outperforms others. Finally, an efficient approach is demonstrated by training a network to solve a range of linear PDEs with pre-trained weights, achieving data-free training in a short amount of time.

This study examines the behavior of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by modeling the interaction between gate voltage and ferroelectric polarization, which gives rise to a negative capacitance effect, as well as exploring the impact of thermal fluctuations. Our analysis reveals that thermal fluctuations can hinder the negative capacitance effect, an observation supported by hysteresis loop simulations. Additionally, we simulate the movement of polarization domains within ferroelectric channels over time, which helps to understand how these structures evolve. Our findings also indicate that smaller FeFETs are more susceptible to negative capacitance and provide a understanding of how thermal fluctuations can be understood using statistical mechanics.

A significant knowledge gap exists in the field of Software Engineering Education (SEED) regarding cargo, particularly in the area of supply-chain security education. Existing Cargo Security Education (CSE) resources are scarce and limited. Through an in-depth evaluation, three existing approaches were identified and compared, which are: (1) vulnerability-based (VB), (2) threat-based (TB), and (3) asset-based (AB). Analysis revealed that VB is the most prevalent approach in current CSE papers, accounting for 62.5% of them. TB and AB each account for 12.5% and 25% respectively. Research into existing CSE practices has shown that VB-focused education primarily addresses cargo ecosystem vulnerabilities such as security updates, package security, and trade-offs between security and performance. TB-based education focuses on cargo security threats like data loss, exposure, and compromise. AB-based education centers on protecting cargo assets like registers and databases. Although VB offers practical insights, TB and AB can promote a more comprehensive understanding of cargo security education. To address this, we present three innovative approaches: (1) task-based (KB), which combines VB and AB and could lead to the creation of more complex and practical educational materials; (2) project-based (PB), which incorporates multiple knowledge areas for a more hands-on learning experience; and (3) community-based (CB), which involves real-world community activities to improve cargo security. These new approaches may enable Cargo Security Education to

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper introduces a new approach to demonstrate irreducibility of stochastic dynamical systems by incorporating both state-dependent mass terms and damping. The obtained result is robust as it does not necessitate detailed knowledge of specific system trajectories. This robustness is illustrated by examining a family of Hamiltonian systems.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This degree corresponds to the fewest number of elements required to generate some of the group's maximal cyclic subgroups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively explored at high-energy colliders. The LHCb experiment, with its unique capability for precision measurements of hadron production and decay at forward rapidity, has started to fill this knowledge gap by collecting data from LHC Run 2 at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. This experiment involved p-p collisions and measured the production of charged hadrons across a wide range of rapidities and pseud rapidities. Additionally, it examined how these measurements change based on the multiplicity of soft particles and how they relate to parton scattering processes.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), have achieved exceptional performance in image recognition but are often hindered by their high computational requirements. This can make them impractical for real-time applications, particularly when paired with fast-moving objects. To address these limitations, this research introduces OCNs (Orientation Convolution Networks), a novel type of convolutional neural network. OCNs utilize compact filters based on oriented rectangles and incorporate a fast, custom convolution algorithm. This approach significantly reduces the computational load and power consumption compared to standard DCNNs. The proposed OCNs are as accurate as their DCNN counterparts in recognition, but up to 100 times faster in inference. Additionally, a new type of filter called a hologram filter has been developed. This filter adapts its shape dynamically to match the input, using a semi-parametric convolution algorithm. The hologram filter enhances the performance of OCNs by roughly 5% with negligible computational cost.

This study focuses on enhancing the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks when applied to point cloud processing. By carefully analyzing and streamlining graph convolutional networks, specifically those used in point cloud segmentation and classification, we can better their scalability. Our research optimizes the structure of these networks to reduce their complexity and improve their performance. This systematic optimization involves standardizing graph convolutional operations and removing redundant components, allowing our networks to learn more effectively from point cloud data.

We introduce a new type of host-hopping Trojan attack that uses fixed images in web pages as a trigger, which can be easily concealed withinlegitimate content. To address this, we developed an automatic approach to detect hidden Trojan triggers by combining novel image processing and machine learning techniques. Our method outperforms existing host-based detection systems in several key aspects, including the ability to detect obfuscated code withinlegitimate content, utilize low-resolution content, and survive trigger encryption. We also propose a new trigger design based on diverse content to improve reliability and reduce obfuscation, which we call camouflage triggering. Our experiments reveal that the hidden Trojans can cause an average 3.5 times more privilege escalation compared to activated ones, while being undetected by leading host-based Anti-Virus solutions on average 95.2% of the time. To complement our detection method, we propose host-free filtering as an alternative to host-based execution, which can effectively prevent the average 99.5% of potential privilege escalation attacks.

We introduce ROSIE IFU, a newly added instrument to the ALMA Complex at the NOEMA site in Italy. This innovative camera captures a 30x30 field of view, with each element in the array covering 10 arcseconds. Each pixel is served by a high-sensitivity detector that operates within a frequency range of 231 to 240 GHz. With spectral resolution options of 2 or 4 pixels per velocity channel, data can be collected at a rate of up to 900 pixels per second. Initial operations have demonstrated a spectral resolution of 2 pixels, with the capability to expand down to 0.5 pixels. By combining the detector array's outputs, a image with 900 pixels can be produced. Each second, this corresponds to a pixel-sized area of 0.011 arcseconds squared. To optimize data handling, a real-time image creation and reorganization algorithm has been developed, allowing adaptability to various observational needs.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck et al. (Eur. Phys. J. A50, 67 (2014)) are considered in relation to more recent double beta decay, isotopic abundance and stellar evolution data. Furthermore, recent outcomes from the Lattice QCD calculation on the B-value and isotopic abundance calculations are also discussed.

A crucial aspect in comprehending the formation and evolution of Earth-like planets is devolatilisation, yet very little is known about the volatiles in terrestrial exoplanets. Research has shown that devolatilisation can have a substantial impact on the bulk composition of super-Earths, complicating the interpretation of their composition and hindering our understanding of their volatile content. We developed a statistical approach to investigate volatiles in terrestrial planets, incorporating the effects of terrestrial evolution and considering multiple formation processes. By applying our model to fictional terrestrial planets around HD 40979, a star known to host several temperate planets, we found that volatile content can be constrained when combined with other constraints on terrestrial composition. Furthermore, our model can be applied to existing datasets, and we have identified HD 40979 b and HD 217107 b as potential candidates for further investigation. To gain insights into volatile content, we propose a multi-faceted approach, including precise radial velocity measurements, high-resolution imaging, and high-resolution spectroscopy, which can be utilised in various scenarios.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), with many using raw CSI data. However, CSI can be distorted by system-specific factors, distorting the feature space and hindering performance. This study investigates how DNNs are affected by system mismatches and demonstrates that using raw CSI can lead to suboptimal localization. Furthermore, we analyze how different architecture choices and training conditions impact the robustness of the trained models and propose a two-stage feature extraction process to mitigate the negative effects of system mismatches and enhance robustness.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A edge coloring of a graph assigns colors to edges such that every edge is given a color.  In strong edge coloring, we ensure that every edge on a path of length two has a unique color.  The minimum number of colors needed for a strong edge coloring of a graph G is called the strong chromatic edge index and denoted by index(G).  In this research, we found the strong chromatic edge index for the following graphs: (1) lexicographic product of graphs, (2) Cartesian product of graphs, (3) Heawood graph, and (4) Petersen graph.

We investigate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the adjacency matrices for the Hamming graphs H(n,q). Our focus is on eigenvalues within the interval [n(q-2), 2n]. The related eigenspaces are demonstrated to possess a cyclic symmetry. Furthermore, we establish the multiplicity of each eigenvalue in this particular eigenvalue spectrum. Building on this, we define the eigenvector E(n,q) and examine its correlations with the standard basis. Our research also extends to relating this to the q-factorization of evaluations of Jack polynomials.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks.
In 2021, the COPASI team released a standalone version specifically for Windows.
This report details our experience installing and setting up this software,
including steps to access an online documentation site and simulate a biochemical
process by modeling a Penicillin production pathway.

Deep neural networks have proven effective in various practical applications, but their widespread adoption is hindered by uncertainties associated with their predictions. Neural networks learn a mapping from inputs to outputs, accompanied by two types of uncertainties - aleatoric and epistemic. To address this, we propose a framework for quantifying both uncertainties in inference, using sharpness-aware weight estimation, a technique that enables weight perturbation to simulate model uncertainty. Our method involves using an auxiliary network, the deep ensembling algorithm, to model uncertainty in inference inputs. As part of the framework, we also develop an efficient approach for sampling from perturbed models without relying on full batch training. Experimental results demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed method in predicting both known and unknown data.

We are investigating quantum deformations of quasi-split Lie supergroups of type A based on supermatrix quantum groups. Thesedeformedquasisplitgroupswillsatisfyaspecificcondition,referredtoastheR-matrixcondition,whichallowsus todemonstratethattheyhaveaspecificstructure,whichcanbedemonstratedbyestablishingacorrespondencebetweentheirfunctionalsandanassociatedquantumgroup.

We examine a method for policy optimization in massive Markov decision processes that involve numerous states and actions, assuming access to a dynamic simulation model. Our approach combines elements of policy gradient estimation with a technique called importance sampling to create an unbiased metric for policy performance. This metric serves as the foundation for a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm that generates weighted samples from the current policy, enabling efficient evaluation without exploring every possible action. This sample method can be executed in a manner similar to standard importance sampling, producing weighted transitions that can be updated recursively. These samples allow us to calculate key components required for improving the policy, which can be executed in a manner similar to batch gradient ascent. Our method has been implemented in a manner similar to REINFORCE, a pioneering algorithm in deep reinforcement learning, which has been shown to perform well in a variety of domains.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish that the symbolic powers of $I(\(\mathcal{D})$ exhibit both ordinary and nearly all Rees valuations. Additionally, for weighted directed trees, the symbolic powers of its edge ideal are equivalent to the ordinary powers. Furthermore, we identify specific weighted directed graphs where the first symbolic power surpasses the first ordinary power. This finding is then extended to ideal quotients of weighted directed graphs, and we determine conditions under which the first symbolic power quotient equals the first quotient of the ordinary power.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem associated with hydrological modeling, specifically the accurate determination of rainfall and runoff data. To achieve this, we developed a computer simulator capable of generating artificial rainfall-runoff sequences based on a hydrological model, with the accuracy dependant on the accuracy of the underlying hydrological model. Consequently, the reliability of our simulator in determining artificial data is contingent on the correctness of the hydrological model used. To facilitate data determination, we applied the multiplicative decomposition principle and created a novel, efficient measurement system for both rainfall and runoff data. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis was conducted to evaluate the stability of the multiplicative decomposition system in relation to various input data errors, and a demonstration of actual data processing was presented using a PC.

Research has shown that certain membership queries can enhance the robustness of learning models, specifically local queries confined to a restricted range. We provide theoretical justification for this finding, showing that analysis of model behavior within this query range is crucial. We also introduce a practical algorithm which provides guarantees on model robustness, answering queries online and also in batches. This has the added benefit of enabling identification of data characteristics that are essential for achieving a specified robustness level. Our experiments, conducted on image classification datasets, validate the efficacy of this algorithm.

Using the CMS experiment at the LHC, fragmentation functions for jets and charged particles were examined in pp and PbPb collisions at 5.02 TeV.  Considering both truth and reconstructed quantities, a varied suppression pattern is observed for charged particles across different jet thresholds, with more significant suppression for smaller jets. The nuclear modification difference between truth and reconstructed quantities indicates a potential overestimation of jet energy loss based on reconstruction alone. Furthermore, fragmentation functions were calculated in a corrected manner, and a more uniform energy loss for jets is observed. At a specific scale of 30 GeV, a 50% energy loss for charged particles was observed, while in another scenario, a 30-40% energy loss for charged particles was observed across all jet scales.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Dyspsis Y1, recently identified as a potential Y dwarf with a predicted temperature of 700-800 K, was actually discovered in an earlier study but misclassified as a brown dwarf due to its unusual color characteristics. Its distinctive color pattern, characterized by unusually red near-infrared indices (J-H, H-K), was inconsistent with typical low-mass stars and brown dwarfs. A typical L/T dwarf would exhibit a 'bluer' H band due to gravitational binding effects. However, the discovery of Y1 was made through its presence in a different, well-studied cluster. Its low-mass, star-like properties were key to understanding its formation and behavior.

The top 10% of events with the highest radial flow in Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions, selected based on charged-particle multiplicity, were examined. These examinations included transverse momentum distributions, Higgs-like scalar and jet-like particle abundances, and total radial flow for all events. It was found that the excess of scalar and total momentum for the top events was well predicted by in-medium quantum chromodynamics calculations. However, this assumption doesn't hold for jet-like outcomes, which were significantly exceeded by simulations. Analysis suggests that the discrepancy arises from an incomplete understanding of high-transverse-momentum tail behavior, specifically the process of parton splitting.

We develop a novel, numerically stable approach to calculating parton distribution functions and split functions through solution of the proton conservation equation using the method of characteristics. This numerical method of PDF evolution is complemented by a approach using a fast Fourier transform. Our approach utilizes boundary values of parton distribution functions at a specific scale. We demonstrate that by applying a matrix-valued differential equation to these boundary values, with solutions connected by split functions, we can obtain solutions for various scales. This method is efficient, as it reduces computations to those necessary for solving one single-scale problem.

Sintered Martian and lunar soil substitutes have exhibited potential as low-cost construction materials for sustainable, 3D-printed habitats on other planets. 3D printing with Martian and lunar soil has been feasible in the laboratory using a fused deposition modeling (FDM) process, which involves melting synthetic regolith and polymer blends. However, 3D printing with actual Martian and lunar soil on-site would not be possible using FDM due to their melting points. We propose an alternative low-cost method involving a modified FDM process that incorporates an additional sintering step at lower printing temperatures, followed by post-processing at temperatures between 700-900 K. Experimental results indicate that this method produces strong and durable samples of Martian and lunar soil, bound together by metallic minerals, which exhibit a minimum compressive strength of 3.5-4.5 MPa after a single layer of printing and minimal water content of <1%. The method's simplicity, minimal equipment requirements, and reduced material toxicity suggest that 3D printing with Martian and lunar soil, bound together by heat, could potentially take place in the future on these celestial bodies.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber are examined within a framework incorporating a slip boundary condition.
First, we establish a thickness profile consistent with the slip boundary condition.
Next, we analyze the effect of liquid-solid slip on the growth of ripples in a film undergoing Rayleigh-Plateau instability.
Our results show that slip boundary conditions promote faster and longer-lasting ripple formation compared to conventional no-slip conditions.
We observe that certain slip parameters allow for complete suppression of decay following initial growth, and even initial increases in viscosity can lead to a growth of perturbations.

This paper classifies a specific category of orbifolds derived from chiral modules associated with simple vector-vector conjugal pairs of rational cocommutative coalgebras, specifically excluding a known set of five coalgebras. We identify four exceptional orbifolds that are also chiral modules, and then complete the classification of the category's auto-equivalences, and further, manually classify a category of orbififles on this category, which allows us to construct a non-trivial module within the category, and finally, determine the structural properties of the category's local modules, which are essential in the rationality criteria for a triangular coassociative coalgebra, and we prove that this rationality occurs if and only if the category's coaction is trivial, and we examine key properties of local modules, and prove that they are closed under various module operations, and we analyze their fusion properties.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher in 1937 to model the spread of a beneficial allele within a population. We attach a probability measure to the solutions of this equation, representing the frequency of a trait within a population that expands at a constant velocity. We employ a probabilistic approach, utilizing branching random walks with exponential growth to characterize the measure's asymptotic behavior. This research focuses on several key aspects, including the frequency of allele fixation at the wave front, its temporal and spatial distribution across the wave front, and the frequency of trait introduction into the population following fixation.

This work addresses the challenge of handwritten mathematical term classification. A U-shaped neural network is utilized to produce a dilated binary map of each input image, where a binary classifier then determines whether the image contains mathematical notation. Following this, a set of key points is identified on the dilated map to segment the input image into distinct regions for further analysis.

This paper addresses duration modeling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by introducing an innovative approach that employs an HMM to model median phoneme durations rather than means, leveraging a mixture-Dirichlet process to minimize assumptions on the underlying phoneme duration probability distributions. This new method has superior performance compared to conventional HMM+Gaussian duration modeling. Furthermore, it demonstrates that incorporating an auxiliary variable for phoneme-aligned breath groups can be beneficial in achieving natural-sounding speech synthesis. A framework is also presented that enables switching between breath groups at the phoneme level without altering HMM states. Evaluation reveals that this approach yields more accurate median phoneme durations, especially for long durations, and produces synthesized speech that sounds as natural as HMM-based speech at a comparable computational cost.

Species distribution models are a fundamental aspect of ecological research.
This study focuses on finding an optimal estimator for species presence.
Unlike previous research, which often relied on assumptions about species habitats,
this study made no such assumptions.
It derived an estimator that utilizes information from an optimal survey plan.
This plan is derived by making assumptions only about the average species presence,
based on readily available data.
This approach results in an estimator with the lowest possible variance among all
estimators based on those observations.
Interestingly, this estimator appears to be more efficient than previously known
estimators that rely on additional species habitat assumptions.
Numerical examples demonstrate the significance of these findings.

A significant advantage of deep learning technologies is their potential to enhance human expertise by reducing the likelihood of diagnostic errors, particularly in the field of dermatology.  The efficacy of this approach has been tested through a novel, interactive learning interface designed to aid physicians in the diagnosis of skin cancer.  This interface combines passive deep learning models with active learning techniques, allowing physicians to actively engage in data annotation and receive real-time diagnostic feedback.  Preliminary studies indicate that this approach leads to noticeable improvements in diagnostic accuracy and self-confidence among physicians.

To identify the essential characteristics of Type Ia supernovae from spectral data, we employ a probabilistic autoencoder with a specialized architecture tailored to incorporate astrophysically relevant parameters. By training this model on spectral time-series information from 114 supernovae, we discover that it learns to separate data into two distinct groups, which correspond to different subclasses of Type Ia supernovae. Furthermore, the model's output can be used to create supervised models that accurately reproduce full broad-band photometry across 1,029 nearby Type Ia supernovae. We compare these models to established spectral-to-light curve models and observe that a simple linear relationship between the physically-parameterized latent space and light curves provides nearly identical results to more complex models using sine basis functions. We also examine whether these basis functions have a relevant physical interpretation.

A massive neutral gas outflow was identified in a star-forming galaxy with heavy dust content. The outflow was discovered using ALMA and NOEMA while studying super-wind phenomena in such galaxies. The outflow has a high expansion speed of 460-650 km/s and involves approximately 16 billion solar masses of gas. The mass of this outflow corresponds to about 20 percent of the galaxy's total molecular gas. The outflow was found to have solar metallicity and no outflow of heavy metals was detected. A dust-obscured galaxy with high redshift was analyzed. The outflow may be related to a super-wind ejected by a central star-forming region in the galaxy. The super-wind could be impacting the surrounding intergalactic space and regulating matter cycling in the galaxy. The findings suggest that mass loss from such galaxies through outflows could be a common phenomenon and have a significant impact on the loss of gas and heavy metals to the surrounding intergalactic space. The super-wind could be interacting with the surrounding intergalactic space and having a significant impact on the galaxy's evolution. The mass of the outflow suggests that a significant amount of gas is escaping the galaxy and could be impacting the loss of mass and gas in the galaxy. Investigations into the dynamics of turbulent plumes with suspended particles were conducted through numerical simulations, examining how the direction of buoyancy fluxes affects fluid entrainment and particle concentration patterns. In conditions of negligible particle Reynolds number and an intermediate range of Arseniev number, where particle relaxation time is a small fraction of the plume scale time, we observed that regardless of whether particles experience positive or negative buoyancy, fluid entrainment rates converge at a similar level, roughly 0.07 in magnitude. Furthermore, our simulations revealed distinct differences in particle concentration distribution, with both types of particles exhibiting a concentration maximum in the region where the most intense turbulence occurs. However, particles with negative buoyancy tend to remain confined within a narrower area compared to their positively buoyant counterparts. Additionally, our simulations revealed an invariable ratio of particle relaxation time to the turbulence's characteristic time, which directly correlates with the plume expansion rate regardless of the direction of particle buoyancy.

Understanding the spread of diseases within networks of individuals in contact has been a long-standing goal in studying epidemics. By mapping disease transmission onto graphs of contacts, researchers have been able to identify key patterns in how outbreaks occur. However, graphs can only represent pairs of individuals in contact, which is a limitation given that groups of people can also interact. By utilizing hyperedges to represent group activities, we can develop a more comprehensive model of how diseases spread. This new model, based on hypergraphs, provides a more detailed description of how outbreaks occur and allows us to see the impact of group sizes on transmission rates. Through simulations, we found that considering the Group Activity Index significantly alters the spread of diseases and that larger groups can have a significant impact on transmission rates. This has important implications for public health measures, as it suggests that activity levels and group sizes should be taken into account when assessing the spread of infectious diseases.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, particularly with the development of sophisticated characterization tools, have fueled interest in manipulating their magnetic properties through an external magnetic field. The specific properties of CrI$_3$, a material exhibiting opposite magnetic behaviors in its ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states, make it an ideal subject for such research. Even a thin layer of CrI$_3$ can exhibit complex behavior when subjected to a magnetic field, a phenomenon that has significant implications for its potential applications. Even more intriguing is the possibility of a magnetic field inducing a transition from a ferromagnetic to an antiferromagnetic state in CrI$_3$. Even a small magnetic field can induce a phenomenon where the spins within the material align in opposite directions, a effect that has significant implications for its potential applications. Understanding this effect is crucial for a deeper understanding of its behavior under a magnetic field. We examine the behavior of solar-stellar rotation at varying levels, using three distinct dynamical regimes characterized by a specific parameter known as the Rossby number. We combine existing data from stellar activity levels, observed magnetic fields, and simulations within dynamo models. The first regime, representing rapidly rotating stars with a low Rossby number, features strong internal rotation variations that may lead to a completely mixed internal structure. The second regime, also characterized by a mid-range Rossby number, is dominated by global magnetic fields, but exhibits uniform stellar rotation. However, stars with higher rotation rates, corresponding to a lower Rossby number, are dominated by differential rotation and weaker global magnetic fields. We leverage these observations and theoretical models to predict evolutionary changes in stellar rotation, noting that an increase in age typically results in smoother and more uniform rotation patterns, as well as weaker global magnetic fields, due to a higher rotation speed.

Deep multimodal learning models need to process various input types, such as text and images.  Current methods heavily rely on cross-modal interactions to fuse different inputs, but they're not well-suited for handling multiple input modes.  This paper introduces the K-fan deep architecture to efficiently tackle problems with several input modes.  It uses independent encoders for each input type and two distinct layers - hybrid pooling and decoding - to fuse different inputs.  We apply the K-fan fan-out approach to create a shared K-fan deep model variant, which significantly reduces computational costs.  Experimental results show that the K-fan fan-out model achieves comparable, if not better, performance than strong baselines in classification tasks involving multiple input modes.

The current approach to software testing, centered on executing individual functions in a thread-safe environment, is insufficient for programs that rely on multi-threading, as it overlooks the program's behavior when running multiple threads simultaneously. Existing testing methods, including unit testing, functional testing, and model checking, have limitations in detecting race conditions, particularly when it comes to programs that use non-deterministic features like random number generation. A proposed solution involves using abstract interpretation to analyze a program's behavior without executing it, focusing on shared variables, their value ranges, and their temporal characteristics.

The widespread use of messaging apps like WhatsApp allows for the rapid dissemination of information, but also facilitates the spread of misinformation, especially in private, centralized groups. Our study focuses on understanding how information spreads in such settings, by combining theoretical modeling with data analysis from both non-misinformation and misinformation groups. We found that once misinformation is introduced, it can spread quickly and persistently, unless actively countered by reliable information. This highlights the importance of addressing misinformation in messaging apps, by disseminating accurate information in a timely manner.

A paper by Dykstra and Tjøstheim's work on age-specific branching populations is discussed, with a focus on their method for analyzing spectral characteristics of populations. Spectral characteristics can be interpreted as a generalization of the average population size and are calculated using an eigenvalue-based approach. However, this approach has a limitation as it's only applicable when the population matrix has a complete set of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. This study generalizes the model proposed by Dykstra and Tjøstheim by considering a complex matrix structure that accounts for both ages and sexes. Despite the increased complexity, the population model retains its triangular form, allowing for the determination of its characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues, and corresponding eigenvectors. This study also establishes conditions for the completeness of the eigenvectors and evaluates the applicability of Fourier analysis in assessing population growth.

The primary goal of a spoofing countermeasure system is to differentiate between genuine and synthesized vocal inputs, which is often used to prevent voice-based authentication systems from being compromised by voice synthesis attacks. We propose a novel neural network-based system that utilizes an attention-based rectified linear unit (AReLU) to enhance its accuracy. The AReLU consists of two crucial components: initial filtering to eliminate irrelevant frequencies and subsequent amplification to increase the contrast between these frequencies. By incorporating contextual information, AReLU yields more precise outcomes than traditional nonlinear units. Experimental results demonstrate that our system achieves a low equal error rate (10.1%) across several languages, outperforming existing spoofing countermeasure systems.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model, offers a framework to understand warping, inflation, and particle unification. However, developing inflationary models in supergravity is complicated by issues with moduli stabilization, which is necessary to produce realistic models from string theory. A new class of supergravity models, known as the 'no-scale' class, can mitigate these challenges, as they inherently stabilize some moduli fields and avoid some destabilizing effects. This work presents an investigation into the most basic no-scale supergravity models, using specific formulations to study inflationary model building. We develop models that incorporate both slow-roll and hybrid inflation and examine how quantum corrections impact these models.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs. An apparatus is developed to isolate this nonreciprocity, and it's demonstrated in various setups including linear and coupled linear cavities coupled with dispersive wave mixers. Two forms of nonreciprocity are observed, including an erasure of an interference pattern and the modulation of interference visibility. These occurrences are consistent with the prediction of a directional visibility switch derived from a mathematical model.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as leading platforms for quantum computing, but flaws in the circuit materials undermine their effectiveness. This study introduces a new measurement technique, critical for capturing quantum states in complex systems. The method employs a quantum sensor, enabling precise measurement of any internal component within coupled quantum circuits. As an initial test, researchers developed a strategy to mitigate defects in superconducting resonators, achieving a major advancement in device performance. This innovation could pave the way for quantum technology applications and further refinement of underlying technologies, including thin-film processing.

We are looking for countable transitive models of set theory where specific statements about Hausdorff's partitioning of the real line into Borel sets, but uncountable cells, are true or false. Our search is complicated by the lack of a clear definition for "specific" in this context.

For many years, commodity trading advisors, particularly those offering pooled funds, have claimed to harness trading strategies to outperform. Their effectiveness has been questioned, with some evidence suggesting that short-term reversal traders may counteract the gains from mean-reversion trading. This study conducts an in-depth analysis of specific CTAs, their strategies, and market impacts. The results show that CTA trading remains partially effective but is more susceptible to losses during periods of high reversal, and traders who incorporate counter-weights appear to be less impacted by these conditions.

Identifying the application protocol in use over an encrypted connection is a challenging task with far-reaching implications for surveillance, monitoring, and security maintenance. Most current approaches fail due to the reliability of this identification solely on a single TCP stream's content. To address this issue, our system is designed to leverage multiple factors, such as the appliance's capacity for parallel processing and the ability to handle various protocols independently, for accurate identification. Our implementation includes a scalable system that can process data at gigabit speeds and is capable of correctly identifying applications in less than 2 seconds.

Electro-magnons, hybrid states formed from the coupling of photons and magnons, are proposed as possible alternative information carriers. The effective control of magnon-qubit interactions through radiation is crucial for implementing a complete quantum protocol. This study presents a method to achieve coherent cross-coupling of a magnon and multiple quantum bits using an optical cavity and two quantum bit sources. The authors demonstrate that super-magnons, composite entities formed from multiple magnons, can also be prepared through the coherent interaction with a quantum bit. The outcomes of their research include a proposed design for a magnon-based memory and a possible approach to generating few-magnon states on demand.

A new approach to federated learning is proposed for training deep neural networks that addresses the issue of non-identifiable data while preserving user privacy. Traditional federated learning methods assume that data is not non-identifiable distribution; however, this assumption is often not the case in practice. By allowing clients to send randomized labels and applying the exponential family auxiliary labeling (EFAL) method, our approach transforms non-identifiable labels into synthetic, uniformly distributed ones. This enables the central server to aggregate models without compromising user privacy. As a result, our method achieves comparable performance to the central server-based training while maintaining the security of sensitive labels.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink channel estimation in multi-user systems that utilize intelligent-reflecting-surfaces, with a focus on systems with a limited number of antennas at each node. Given that direct signal propagation between antennas is impossible, our model takes into account only the reflected signals that reach the central hub from user equipment, with these signals containing information from both reflected and direct paths from the antennas. Building on this, we develop a new estimation technique that utilizes a sparsifying transform to separate and estimate the relevant channel components. Our approach outperforms existing methods in various scenarios, including those with many IRS antennas, by accurately capturing the channel structure and by space-filling the relevant channel entries.

This study analyzes a comprehensive dataset of online local news articles from across the US, covering nearly 750 markets between January 2020 and April 2021, to examine how COVID-19 was reported in relation to regional characteristics and changing mortality rates at the national level. The research reveals that initial reporting trends were influenced by the overall death rate, but this correlation diminished as government communications and expert advice began to emphasize personal behavior changes. During the early stages, reports focused heavily on the disease itself, yet this was later supplanted by stories highlighting vaccination efforts. Notably, a substantial portion of articles were found to be from just 22 out of 1155 covered markets.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of how humans learn,
yet the specific processes underlying this ability remain elusive. Instead,
research has focused on counting behaviors, often relying on infinite mathematical
models that are inaccessible to the brain. Infinitely learnable theories are
also impractical for counting. To address this, we apply finite learnability
theories from formal language and introduce a new, infinite structure that is
practically learnable by counting even non-primitive terms. We identify a
critical inflection point where counting becomes easier as terms become more
complex, enabling term structure exploitation to learn counting beyond
primitivity. Furthermore, this ability to count non-primitive terms provides
a concrete explanation for why counting terms is more effective than counting
values, offering insights into the cognitive mechanisms behind counting learning.

Bloom filters offer quick assessment of whether an element belongs to a set, but they suffer from a false positive drawback, meaning they may incorrectly suggest inclusion. A more space-efficient solution, the cuckoo filter, doesn't have this limitation, yet it demands more time for verification and has a longer setup time. A revised version of the cuckoo filter optimizes space usage, significantly reduces initial preparation time, and has comparable accuracy to a standard Bloom filter in terms of false positives.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our K\"ahler setup leads to the relationship that mixed volumes correspond to positive products. This analogy enables us to establish a series of K\"ahler inequalities, including the Convex Geometry Conjecture proposed by Abreu and the application of the algebraic proof strategy to the analytic context. Additionally, our findings support existing results like the Brunn-Minkowski inequality for semi-pluristable bodies and the non-arithmeticity of general abelian varieties.

A new approach aims to derive market trend indicators that can predict future price movements based on the volume of shares traded per unit of time, building on concepts of order flow and trade activity. This methodology is then applied to create a trading strategy that seeks to maximize returns while minimizing the effects of market transactions. Results from testing the developed indicators and a basic trading strategy on liquidity stocks from the Warsaw Stock Exchange over a four-year period (2016-2019) using an exhaustive search within a specified timeframe show that the approach may yield higher returns compared to using traditional indicators, particularly during times of market volatility.

This paper presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that addresses both malicious attacks and data privacy concerns. Byzantine-gradient verification allows us to filter out outliers, enhancing model security, but it compromises user privacy. To preserve privacy, we modify this process by applying differential privacy to the verification step, creating a self-sustaining training loop that iterates between aggregation, verification, and local re-training. Our approach, which utilizes precise distance metrics to measure gradient variations, ensures accurate model updates and significantly reduces the need for adjustments in other aggregation methods. Additionally, experiments show that FLVoogd produces more accurate models compared to a control group without verification, demonstrating the technique's effectiveness.

We present a novel framework for autonomous vehicle development, centered around
supervised imitation of expert human drivers. This framework leverages
reinforcement learning to acquire the driving skills, with the agent's objectives
defined by the tasks it needs to complete. The framework employs an autonomous
driving environment, allowing it to be training the agent to steer the vehicle along
a course while avoiding obstacles. Surprisingly, we discovered that agents taught
to mimic human behavior can be effectively utilized to guide reinforcement learning
processes, producing better outcomes more quickly than traditional methods that rely
on random initial actions.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincing deepfakes, which have sparked interest in areas such as entertainment, security, and political communication. Although multiple deepfake creation techniques have been proposed, few studies have addressed the development of deepfakes for animals, which are crucial for assessing the potential risks associated with deepfake adoption, particularly in relation to animal welfare and food security. This research presents a novel deepfake approach that can alter videos of real people and animals by blending their features with those of mask models, which are then integrated into the source video through a process involving a content mask. This technique, which involves two neural networks with two convolutional layers each, has demonstrated its potential through a comparison of original and altered videos, which were evaluated using three metrics: PSNR, SSIM, and MSE.

The discovery of K2-38b sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets orbiting within the habitable zones of their host stars raises inquiries about their potential habitability. To address this, we investigated how stellar X-ray and extreme ultraviolet irradiation affects the atmospheric escape and subsequent evolution of such exoplanets. To model the loss of atmosphere and subsequent evolution, we simulated the initial high mass and various orbital configurations. We found that sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets in habitable zones can experience substantial atmospheric loss, up to 90%, and we established relationships between the final mass and initial mass, orbital distance, and stellar X-ray to Far ultraviolet to Far infrared flux ratio. We discovered that while the bulk of atmospheric loss occurs during the host star's high X-ray emitting youth, it is the photodissociation of water that limits the loss. We examined the potential for these exoplanets to retain water oceans and found that in certain orbital configurations, the majority of water is lost, leaving behind rocky cores with thick CO2 atmospheres. However, in other scenarios, these exoplanets can retain their oceans, with surface temperatures and pressures supporting liquid water. We also evaluated the water loss for other sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets with characterized atmospheres and discovered that in all cases, the bulk of water is lost, with end states featuring water-poor atmospheres.

A model of a learning brain, which can be understood as a system that learns sequences of events, was explored through a study of two types of neurons that learn in groups. It was discovered that through a process of changing the connections between these neurons, a learned sequence of events can be represented as a specific pattern of activity. This pattern can be actively or passively maintained and can also predict upcoming events. What's more, it was found that a particular type of connection between the neurons, known as asymmetric connectivity, is both necessary and sufficient for representing multiple sequences. Lastly, a relationship was identified between the complexity of a sequence and the specific characteristics of the connection between the neurons.

This paper presents a novel approach to character-level scene text recognition by treating it as a self-supervised learning task. Existing OCR models depend on labeled data but struggle with text types not seen during training, leading to overfitting. Our method eliminates the need for annotations by leveraging an attention-based model to crop images containing text, followed by a transformer-based character recognizer trained through a contrastive loss against an unsupervised reference. Experiments demonstrate that our model excels in character recognition and achieves superior performance on the total character accuracy metric, outperforming baseline models with annotated datasets.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states, thereby establishing a framework for estimating probability distributions of values at specific points in time or space. This paper builds on that method by developing a new approach for estimating the probability distributions of temporal and spatial variables themselves.

The increasing prevalence of highly complex systems in industrial settings necessitates advanced analytical tools to monitor and maintain their performance.  Although not explicitly defined in this paper, high-dimensional data presents several inherent monitoring difficulties that can be addressed in various monitoring strategies.  This paper focuses on detecting significant changes in data characteristics that are often overlooked in conventional methods.  To tackle this challenge, a generalized approach is introduced, allowing users to specify the type of data shift they wish to identify.  The method is adaptable to various scenarios, including linear and nonlinear datasets, and can be applied to both labeled and unlabeled data.  The method is illustrated through several case studies involving real-world industrial applications.

We have created a detailed analysis of the Milky Way's accreted galaxies Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 by constructing likelihood functions for their infall timescales and energies. Our study reveals that the probabilities of these galaxies originating from accreted systems are highly probable, with our data supporting this view. Our research indicates that the GSE system's characteristics are consistent with those of a galaxy that fell into the Milky Way approximately 10 billion years ago with an initial velocity of around 350-400 km/s, whereas the Wukong system's characteristics resemble those of a galaxy fall approximately 11 billion years ago with an initial velocity of around 300 km/s. Our data show that while GSE's energy distribution follows a pattern similar to that observed in certain high-velocity clusters of galaxies, the energy distribution of Wukong is more similar to that of certain spiral galaxies. Our study highlights the unique roles played by these two accreted systems in the evolution of the Milky Way and underscores the need for further research into similar accreted systems.

Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills specific criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG[[G]]} for an S[[G]]-module X. When X's constituents meet a finiteness requirement, a homotopy orbit spectral sequence is present, with convergence towards X_{hG[[G]]}, and r-th terms related to the continuous homology of G with coefficients in the r-th constituent of X. For an integer d, a condition on d leads to a specific scenario where these t-terms are of finite type for all t greater than d. In this case, a proposed formula for these tr-values is a significant finding.

The extraction of critical information from digital documents, particularly documents with a complex layout, has gained significant attention. However, most existing methods either concentrate on simple document formats or require training data, which is difficult to obtain and maintain for the diverse set of documents that exist. To overcome these challenges, a new approach is presented that utilizes unsupervised training and a novel framework, called LayoutTransformer, to group document regions by their structural importance. Through unsupervised learning, a document layout is represented as a set of grouped structures, each of which can be trained independently to improve overall performance. The results indicate that the model can be applied effectively to multiple tasks, including element classification and key-value pair extraction, and that it generally produces positive results when compared to existing methods.

The EuS/InAs interface is of significant importance in the research of spin electronics, particularly in the manipulation of spin current and giant magnetoresistance. The interaction at this interface significantly impacts the properties of magnetoelectronics devices, thus making the investigation of its characteristics vital. Using various bonding configurations, such as flat, hcp, and ccp, we have calculated the electronic structure properties, including the energy band offsets and work functions. Our calculations indicate that the Fermi level positions relative to the conduction and valence bands in both materials suggest metallic bonding character. Additionally, we have compared our results with existing experimental data and found that they are in reasonable agreement. Our findings also demonstrate that variations in bonding configurations can lead to distinct electronic structures, emphasizing the significance of precise control over these structures.

A classification of subsets of Baire space based on their Borel Wadge hierarchy has been established. This comprehensive framework includes not only the traditional Borel sets but also specific classes such as analytic sets and certain multivalued preimages. It provides an in-depth understanding of these sets, particularly in relation to Martin-Isbell and Laver sets, by offering precise descriptions of their positions within the Borel Wadge classes.

We introduce ClickTrain, a groundbreaking training framework for visually-grounded language tasks, including Region Language Modeling. This approach synchronizes word information with image regions to optimize the network's representation of textual and spatial data. By leveraging a sparse, structured sampling strategy and multi-task design, ClickTrain facilitates dense matrix operations and reduces redundant computations. Our comparisons with existing supervised frameworks reveal ClickTrain's superior performance. Furthermore, our experiments clickBERT, combining clickTrain with the language model BERT, have yielded industry-leading results in image retrieval and visual language understanding benchmarks, outperforming competing solutions such as R2N1 and RLB by a substantial margin.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from non-commutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying a Theorem that links syntax to semantics, we establish a comprehensive characterisation of multiple modal logics based on the principles of Lambek calculus.

The collaboration between gravitational wave and electromagnetic observatories has the potential to identify several types of compact binary mergers including black hole - black hole, neutron star - neutron star, and neutron star - black hole mergers. Real-time or near real-time cross-correlation of these datasets could provide accurate estimates of astrophysical parameters and fundamental properties. This research focuses on establishing a framework for detecting a particular transient electromagnetic signal in real-time, using data from the LSST, and considering a specific case where real-time optical data from the LSST is paired with gravitational wave data from LIGO-Virgo for a neutron star-field binary merger event.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star significantly colder than the Sun. This exoplanet, which has been confirmed through multiple methods including radial velocity and direct imaging, exhibits a unique characteristic in that its orbit lies unusually close to its parent star. Furthermore, research into this exoplanet has also provided insight into its parent star's metal content, which is notably lower than the Sun's. This finding is particularly significant in the context of existing data which has established a link between metal-rich stars and the prevalence of gas giants. This discovery may therefore provide a clearer understanding of how metal content influences the formation of giant exoplanets. This discovery, which has been published in The Astronomical Journal, has been made possible through a combination of data from multiple sources including the VLT, Keck telescopes and ALMA.

A single agent decision making problem under restrictions can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP), an extension of the standard Markov decision process. Operations research and operations management researchers have extensively studied this, although they have primarily focused on specific problem types with known structures to derive optimal solutions. This paper examines a more complex scenario where an researcher doesn't have access to the underlying model and has to work within the constraints. We propose a constraint satisfaction algorithm that leverages statistical analysis to identify a near-optimal policy, demonstrating its efficacy through experiments.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols, beginning with the process of image segmentation. The complexity of handwritten mathematical expressions makes segmenting them a challenging task. The difficulty arises because individual symbols can appear to overlap, rendering traditional classification techniques ineffective. To tackle this issue, a new approach is proposed that employs a distance transform to identify potential symbol boundaries. The method involves using a template-based pattern matcher to classify regions and a graph optimization algorithm to resolve the task. The proposed method demonstrates promising results when applied to segmented mathematical images.

A proposed method to apply twisted differential geometry to superconformal quantum mechanics is explored, with its underlying mechanism explained in detail. A specific instance of this approach is demonstrated through the example of a resolved conifold, where BPS states are linked to altered Dolbeault cohomology classes. A quantum group structure in this model gives rise to a deformed twisted cohomology, in turn explaining the appearance of non-integer BPS masses within the framework.

We investigate the role of network architecture in the prevalence of contagion, starting with stochastic Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible models. Our analysis reveals that heterogeneous network structures do not consistently support higher epidemic levels than homogeneous networks. Furthermore, random network structures do not always lead to higher susceptibility to outbreaks. To explain these findings, a simplified mean-field model is introduced, which can be applied to various contagion processes. This simplified model is then used to analyze different processes, including Poisson process-driven contagion, and it is found that both the susceptibility to large outbreaks and the size of the largest outbreak can be higher in networks with variable node degrees but lower epidemic levels in networks with heterogeneous structures.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning techniques have proven effective in generating
high-quality actions, but their sample efficiency can be limited. We propose 
incorporating Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a sample-efficient algorithm, into the 
critic component of these methods. By integrating Hamiltonian Monte Carlo within 
the critic, our approach can sample more effectively and improve policy evaluation, 
resulting in superior sample efficiency, particularly in scenarios where 
computational resources are limited. This hybrid algorithm demonstrates 
significantly better performance compared to existing actor-critic techniques 
like TRPO, PPO, and TI3, as demonstrated in various benchmark tests.

Investigating the structure of Mersenne primes above 5 necessitates an examination of their relationship to numbers conforming to the form $6k \pm 1$. We seek a recursive formula that determines whether a Mersenne prime is of the form $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. Our research also entails an exploration of other prime numbers of the form $6k \pm 1$. Specifically, we look at primes in the structure $49k \pm 1$ and $13 \cdot 6^k \pm 1$. Furthermore, we consider whether there is a inherent connection to Wolstenholme primes.

Autonomous navigation of robots in diverse environments is a complex task, 
especially when considering the potential failure of typical sensors due to 
extreme weather conditions. This research addresses the issue of robust 
navigation for robots in conditions where textures and colors may be difficult to 
detect, and where lighting may be insufficient. In situations where 
traditional sensor performance may be compromised, we explore the use of 
thermographic data in place of standard RGB images. Thermographic sensors can 
effectively detect and process target objects and environmental features, 
even in the absence of lighting. However, existing control methods that rely on 
image features in RGB may struggle to operate efficiently in thermographic 
images due to the lack of texture. This study investigates the possibility of 
using thermographic data to control a mobile robot's navigation using a 
model-free reinforcement learning approach, specifically through the 
demonstration of a thermographic vision-controlled robot.

A comprehensive analysis of a peculiar cosmic object, designated as GCMG 1-18, has been conducted using a large 14.6-meter telescope and a high-resolution spectrograph. This study reveals a significant spectral shift in the object, accompanied by an unusual flat spectrum. To better understand this phenomenon, a thorough examination of similar cosmic bodies and a comprehensive radiative transfer analysis have been carried out. Multiple potential explanations for this spectral variation have been explored, including complex organic compounds, cosmic metallic materials and their molecular counterparts, as well as ices of volatile substances. Interestingly, a particular type of dispersed cosmic dust model, consisting of an intermediate between traditional stardust and space ices, has been found to accurately reproduce both the object's continuum and spectral features. This suggests that a similar substance with a composition similar to water, in a disordered state, could be present in other cosmic bodies and objects.

Let $\mathcal{R}_n$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of size $n \times n$ over a field of size $q$. This article investigates the properties of submodules within $\mathcal{R}_n$ considered as a module over itself. Specifically, it focuses on non-free cyclic submodules of rank one, which are obtained by multiplying a non-zero matrix of $\mathcal{R}_n$ with a specific matrix of $\mathcal{R}_n$ consisting of a single non-zero entry. The article establishes a one-to-one correspondence between points in an affine plane of size $q^{n-1}$ and distinct non-free cyclic submodules of $\mathcal{R}_n$ that are not annihilated by any non-zero element of $\mathcal{R}_n$. The article further examines the properties of submodules that can be represented as free modules.
